Long term tidal constituents for NOAA tide gauges

Source: R/data.R
long_term_tidal_constituents.Rd

Harmonic constituents of long term tidal amplitude changes for NOAA tide gauges. 4.4 and 18.6 year cycles in tidal amplitude change are accounted for following formulas presented in Peng et al. (2018). Formulas are modified to fit harmonic constituents to different tidal flood and ebb types matching annual_compiled_datums.

Usage

long_term_tidal_constituents

Format

A data frame with 1000 rows and 17 columns:

station_id

Unique numeric NOAA station identifier

station_name

Unique NOAA station name

start_date

Calendar start date for observation (YYYYMMDD)

end_date

Calendar end date for observation (YYYYMMDD)

tide

Type of tide: HHA=Higher High Annual, HOT=Highest Observed Tide, MSL=Mean Sea Level, LLA=Lower Low Annual, LOT=Lowest Observed Tide, HHS=Higher High Spring, HH=Higher High Daily, LH=Lower High Daily, HL=Higher Low Daily, LL=Lower Low Daily, LLS=Lower Low Spring

mean_amp

Mean tidal amplitude for model 1 (4.4 and 18.6 year cycles accounted for)

amp18

18.6 year cycle amplitude of amplitude for model 1 (4.4 and 18.6 year cycles accounted for)

phase18

18.6 year cycle phase for model 1 (4.4 and 18.6 year cycles accounted for)

amp44

4.4 year cycle amplitude for model 1

phase44

4.4 year cycle phase for model 1

rse

Residual standard error for model 1 (4.4 and 18.6 year cycles accounted for)

r2

R-squared value for model 1 (4.4 and 18.6 year cycles accounted for)

mean_ampb

Mean tidal amplitude for model 2 (18.6 year cycle accounted for)

amp18b

18.6 year cycle amplitude of amplitude for model 2 (18.6 year cycle accounted for)

phase18b

18.6 year cycle phase for model 2 (18.6 year cycle accounted for)

rseb

Residual standard error for model 2 (18.6 year cycle accounted for)

r2b

R-squared value for model 2 (18.6 year cycle accounted for)

Source

Peng, D., Hill, E. M., Meltzner, A. J., & Switzer, A. D. (2019). Tide gauge records show that the 18.61‐year nodal tidal cycle can change high water levels by up to 30 cm. Journal of Geophysical Research: Oceans, 124(1), 736-749.

Recalculated in https://github.com/Smithsonian/Tidal_Scenarios, by James Holmquist
